A breast cancer that lacks the three receptors (oestrogen, progesterone, HER2) that other breast cancers can be treated through. It was the hardest subtype for decades; since 2020 immunotherapy and ADCs have changed that. [1] TNBC is defined by what it lacks: ER <1%, PR <1%, HER2 0-1+ (or 2+/ISH-negative). [1] It is biologically heterogeneous (basal-like 1 and 2, mesenchymal, luminal androgen receptor, immunomodulatory subtypes), nearly always TP53-mutant, frequently HRD-positive (~20% germline BRCA1/2), and has the highest TROP2 expression and the most immune infiltration of any breast subtype. [1] Curative-intent: chemo-immunotherapy (KEYNOTE-522) cures more patients than ever; pCR ~65%. Adjuvant PARP inhibitor for BRCA carriers. [1] Treatments in the standard of care for TNBC on OnCo include Pembrolizumab, Carboplatin, Olaparib, Sacituzumab govitecan and Datopotamab deruxtecan. [1] A growth-signal receptor. Some cancers make far too much of it, and drugs that block it or use it as a docking site have transformed those cancers. [2] The hormone switch that drives most breast cancers. Blocking or destroying it is the oldest and most effective targeted therapy. [3]

[2] HER2 (https://onco.cc/targets/her2/)

A breast cancer that lacks the three receptors (oestrogen, progesterone, HER2) that other breast cancers can be treated through. It was the hardest subtype for decades; since 2020 immunotherapy and ADCs have changed that. [1] Stage I (T1a-b N0): Surgery ± radiation; chemotherapy for ≥T1c; TIL-high tumours have >90% 5-year RFS even without chemotherapy (OPTimal, ETNA, TIL-CHOICE cohorts). De-escalation trials ongoing. [1] Stage II-III: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab + carboplatin/paclitaxel → AC/EC, surgery, adjuvant pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE-522). Germline BRCA + residual disease: olaparib 1 year (OlympiA). Residual disease without BRCA: capecitabine (CREATE-X). Radiation per stage. [1] Metastatic, first line, PD-L1 CPS ≥10: Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-355) or sacituzumab govitecan + pembrolizumab (ASCENT-04, approved 2026). [1] Metastatic, first line, PD-L1 negative or PD-1 ineligible: Datopotamab deruxtecan (TROPION-Breast02, OS benefit) or sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT-03), both approved 2026; PARP inhibitor if germline BRCA; chemotherapy. [1] Metastatic, later lines: Whichever TROP2 ADC was not used first (cross-resistance uncertain); T-DXd if HER2-low (DESTINY-Breast04); iza-bren where available; chemotherapy (eribulin, capecitabine); clinical trials. [1] In the pipeline for TNBC: Sacituzumab tirumotecan, Izalontamab brengitecan, TROPION-Breast05, IZABRIGHT-Breast01, OptimICE-pCR (A012103) and SCARLET (SWOG S2212). [1]

[1] Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (https://onco.cc/cancers/tnbc/)

The first TROP2-targeted ADC. It delivers a strong chemotherapy directly to breast and bladder cancer cells and is now a first-line option in triple-negative breast cancer. [1] The side effects recorded for Sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT, Trodelvy arm, n=258), most serious first: neutropenia (78% any grade, 49% grade 3 or higher); diarrhoea (59% any grade, 11% grade 3 or higher); anaemia (94% any grade, 9% grade 3 or higher); fatigue (65% any grade, 6% grade 3 or higher); nausea (57% any grade, 3.1% grade 3 or higher). [1] Monitoring: Blood counts each dose; UGT1A1*28 homozygotes have earlier and more frequent neutropenia; anti-emetic premedication. [1] Dose changes: Hold and reduce for grade 3-4 neutropenia or diarrhoea; G-CSF prophylaxis permitted. [1]

Trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu) is the most successful ADC ever. It redefined HER2 by working in tumours with only tiny amounts of the protein, and in 2026 moved into early-stage breast cancer. [1] It is an ADC: Trastuzumab backbone; DXd released by lysosomal cathepsins; TOP1 inhibition and bystander diffusion. [1] In the United Kingdom, Trastuzumab deruxtecan is approved by the MHRA (first approval 2021). [1] It is also approved in the United States (FDA, 2019), the European Union (EMA / European Commission, 2021), Japan (PMDA / MHLW, 2020), China (NMPA, 2023) and Australia (TGA, 2022). [1] Approvals recorded on OnCo: US 2022, HER2-low metastatic breast cancer; HER2-mutant NSCLC; US 2024, HER2 IHC3+ solid tumours (tumour-agnostic); US 2025, HER2-low/ultralow HR+ breast cancer after endocrine therapy (DESTINY-Breast06); US 2026, Early-stage HER2+ breast cancer (neoadjuvant and post-neoadjuvant). [1] Latest regulatory event: 2026-Q2, approval (US): Early-stage HER2+ breast cancer: neoadjuvant (DESTINY-Breast11) and post-neoadjuvant residual disease (DESTINY-Breast05). [1] Sevabertinib is an oral HER2 inhibitor for lung cancers with HER2 mutations, approved in November 2025 as an alternative to Enhertu and zongertinib. [2]

Sources
[1] Trastuzumab deruxtecan (https://onco.cc/drugs/trastuzumab-deruxtecan/)
[2] Sevabertinib (https://onco.cc/drugs/sevabertinib/)

The most widely used cancer immunotherapy, approved in more than 40 settings, including before and after surgery for triple-negative breast cancer. [1] Humanised IgG4 blocking PD-1; restores T-cell effector function. [1] Step by step: 1) Antibody binds PD-1 on T cells; 2) PD-1/PD-L1 engagement between T cell and tumour is blocked; 3) Exhausted tumour-reactive T cells regain effector function; 4) Interferon-γ and cytotoxic granules are released at the tumour; 5) Tumour cells are killed; memory T cells persist. [1] Inhibitory receptor on activated T cells; ligands PD-L1/PD-L2. Tumour PD-L1 expression, TMB, and MSI predict response imperfectly. [2] The first head-to-head trial in which a new drug beat Keytruda, in China; a survival benefit followed in 2026. [3] The global test of whether ivonescimab plus chemotherapy beats the Keytruda-chemotherapy standard. [4]

A hazard ratio is a number comparing the rate of bad events in two groups. An HR of 0.5 means the risk is halved at any moment. [1] From Cox proportional hazards models. [1] HR <1 favours the experimental arm; confidence interval excluding 1 indicates statistical significance. [1] Why it matters: it comes up in Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. [1] A hazard ratio of 0.70 means that at any given moment patients on the new treatment had 30% less risk of the event (death, progression) than those on the comparison. [2]

Pancreatic cancer is the deadliest common cancer. Almost every tumour carries a KRAS mutation, and for the first time drugs against it are in pivotal trials. [1] Trials on OnCo linked to Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: RASolute 302 (positive), NAPOLI 3 (positive), PRODIGE 24 / CCTG PA6 (positive), PANOVA-3 (positive), Low-dose olanzapine for cancer anorexia (Tata Memorial) (positive) and Ponsegromab phase 2 in cancer cachexia (positive). [1] The trial that nearly doubled survival in previously treated pancreatic cancer, presented in the ASCO 2026 plenary. The biggest result in the disease's history. [2] The first head-to-head trial of the two chemotherapy backbones, won narrowly by the four-drug regimen. [3] Showed that giving the strong four-drug chemotherapy after pancreatic surgery adds years of life for fit patients. [4] The first drug that blocks all active RAS variants, approved by the FDA in August 2026 for metastatic pancreatic cancer, where KRAS drives 90% of tumours. [5] A four-drug chemotherapy combination built on liposomal irinotecan extended survival in metastatic pancreatic cancer by about two months compared with the most widely used doublet, the first positive first-line trial in a decade. [6]

Tumours with a little HER2 (IHC 1+ or 2+ without amplification), or a trace (ultralow), which older HER2 drugs ignored but Enhertu can attack. [1] HER2-low: IHC 1+ or 2+/ISH-negative (~50% of breast cancers, ~35% of TNBC). [1] HER2-ultralow: IHC 0 with membrane staining in ≤10% of cells. [1] Why it matters: it decides or shapes the use of Trastuzumab deruxtecan, and it comes up in HR-positive / HER2-negative breast cancer and TNBC. [1] It created the HER2-low category. [2] Roughly half of all breast cancers are HER2-low, so the trial redefined HER2 testing and opened ADC therapy to a very large population. [2] DESTINY-Breast06, Progression-free survival, HER2-low (BICR): Trastuzumab deruxtecan 13.2 months versus Chemotherapy (TPC) 8.1 months, hazard ratio 0.62, p <0.0001. [3]

A scan that shows where a radioactive tracer accumulates, so it images what tumours are doing rather than what they look like. [1] A CT scan is a fast 3D X-ray that shows the size and shape of tumours and whether they have spread. [2] Principle of PET: Positron-emitting isotopes (18F, 68Ga, 89Zr, 64Cu) attached to a targeting molecule; coincidence detection of 511 keV photons; standardised uptake value (SUV) quantifies uptake. [1] Principle of CT: A rotating X-ray source and detector measure attenuation, which is reconstructed into cross-sectional images. [2] Since of PET: 1975. [1] Since of CT: 1971. [2] Status of PET: standard-of-care. [1] Strengths of PET: Whole-body biology in one scan; Quantitative. [1] Strengths of CT: Fast, ubiquitous; Sub-millimetre resolution. [2] Limitations of PET: Resolution ~4 mm; Tracer supply and cost. [1] Limitations of CT: Anatomic only; cannot distinguish scar from live tumour; Radiation dose. [2]

Sources
[1] PET (positron emission tomography) (https://onco.cc/technologies/pet/)
[2] CT (computed tomography) (https://onco.cc/technologies/ct/)

Any treatment that works by getting the patient's own immune system to attack the cancer, rather than attacking the cancer directly. It can produce responses that last for years, but only in some patients. [1] The main forms are checkpoint inhibitors (antibodies that release the brakes on T cells), cell therapies (CAR-T, TCR-T and TIL, in which a patient's T cells are removed, engineered or expanded, and returned), bispecific T-cell engagers, cancer vaccines including personalised mRNA vaccines, cytokines, and oncolytic viruses. [1] Because the immune system has memory, responses can persist long after treatment stops, which is why the survival curves for melanoma and lung cancer now show a plateau of long-term survivors; the flip side is autoimmune side effects and the fact that many tumours remain 'cold' and unresponsive. [1]

[1] Immunotherapy (https://onco.cc/terms/immunotherapy-term/)

No invasive cancer left in the breast and lymph nodes when the surgeon removes the tissue after pre-surgery treatment. [1] Strongly prognostic in TNBC and HER2+ breast cancer (patients with pCR have ~90% 5-year EFS). [1] Accepted for accelerated approval of neoadjuvant regimens. [1] Why it matters: it comes up in Bladder & urothelial cancer, Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, HER2-positive breast cancer and Oesophageal cancer. [1] Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells by damaging their DNA or the machinery of division. [2] Trials now test de-escalating therapy after pCR (OptimICE-pCR) and escalating for residual disease. [1] Given in cycles to let normal tissue recover, chemotherapy cures some cancers outright (testicular cancer, many lymphomas and childhood leukaemias), prevents recurrence after surgery, and controls advanced disease; it remains the backbone that newer drugs are added to. HER2-positive breast cancer was once the most aggressive subtype and is now one of the most treatable, thanks to trastuzumab and, more recently, Enhertu. [1] Early stage: Neoadjuvant THP or T-DXd → surgery → trastuzumab/pertuzumab (pCR) or T-DXd/T-DM1 (residual). [1] Metastatic: T-DXd + pertuzumab first line (DESTINY-Breast09); tucatinib + trastuzumab + capecitabine for brain metastases; palbociclib maintenance if HR+. [1] Stage I (≤2-3 cm, node-negative): Surgery then weekly paclitaxel × 12 + trastuzumab × 1 year (APT); T-DM1 × 17 cycles is an alternative (ATEMPT). Endocrine therapy if HR+. [1] Stage II-III, neoadjuvant: TCHP (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab, pertuzumab) or anthracycline-taxane + HP; from 2026, T-DXd × 4 → THP (DESTINY-Breast11, pCR 67%). PET-adapted chemotherapy omission (PHERGain) in trials. [1] Post-neoadjuvant, pathologic complete response: Complete 1 year of trastuzumab (± pertuzumab if node-positive at diagnosis); endocrine therapy if HR+; radiation per stage. [1] Post-neoadjuvant, residual invasive disease: T-DXd (DESTINY-Breast05, iDFS HR 0.47 vs T-DM1; approved 2026) replacing T-DM1 (KATHERINE); consider extended adjuvant neratinib for HR+ high-risk. [1] In the pipeline for HER2-positive breast cancer: HER2 PET, Zanidatamab, Disitamab vedotin, Trastuzumab rezetecan, Trastuzumab brengitecan and ARX788. [1]

Sources
[1] HER2-positive breast cancer (https://onco.cc/cancers/breast-her2-positive/)

A breast cancer that lacks the three receptors (oestrogen, progesterone, HER2) that other breast cancers can be treated through. It was the hardest subtype for decades; since 2020 immunotherapy and ADCs have changed that. [1] TNBC is defined by what it lacks: ER <1%, PR <1%, HER2 0-1+ (or 2+/ISH-negative). [1] It is biologically heterogeneous (basal-like 1 and 2, mesenchymal, luminal androgen receptor, immunomodulatory subtypes), nearly always TP53-mutant, frequently HRD-positive (~20% germline BRCA1/2), and has the highest TROP2 expression and the most immune infiltration of any breast subtype. [1] Curative-intent: chemo-immunotherapy (KEYNOTE-522) cures more patients than ever; pCR ~65%. Adjuvant PARP inhibitor for BRCA carriers. [1] Treatments in the standard of care for TNBC on OnCo include Pembrolizumab, Carboplatin, Olaparib, Sacituzumab govitecan and Datopotamab deruxtecan. [1] TNBC accounts for about 10-15% of breast cancers, roughly 200,000 cases per year worldwide, and is more common in younger women, Black women, and BRCA1 carriers. [1]
